questions.stem: How is a fix by cross bearings obtained?
options: From one bearing and the ship's speed
From a single bearing of a floating buoy
Where two or more bearing lines cross
From the ship's DR position alone
questions.explanation: Each bearing gives a line of position. Two lines cross at a fix, and a third line checks them.

questions.stem: A lighthouse bears 072 degrees true from the ship. How is the line of position plotted?
options: From the lighthouse along 072 degrees, away from the ship
From the DR position along 252 degrees
Through the DR position along 072 degrees
Through the light, toward the ship, on 252
questions.explanation: The bearing is the direction from the ship to the object, so the ship lies on the opposite side of the object. The line is drawn from the object along the reciprocal (072 + 180 = 252).

questions.stem: The ship is heading 100 degrees C with a compass error of 14 degrees E. A lighthouse bears 316 degrees C. What true bearing is plotted?
options: 302 degrees
316 degrees
330 degrees
350 degrees
questions.explanation: Compass to true: add easterly error, 316 + 14 = 330. Subtracting (302) is the true-to-compass direction, and 316 is the uncorrected bearing.

questions.stem: Which choice of objects for two bearings gives the best fix?
options: Two objects whose bearings differ by about 15 degrees
Two objects nearly in line on opposite sides
The two nearest buoys regardless of angle
Two fixed marks about 90 degrees apart
questions.explanation: A 90-degree cut gives the smallest fix error for a given bearing error. Lines crossing at a small angle, or nearly in line, make the fix very sensitive to error.

questions.stem: For the same bearing errors, how does a fix with a 30 degree angle of cut compare with one at 90 degrees?
options: It is the same
It is about half as far out
It is about twice as far out
It is about 30 times as far out
questions.explanation: The error varies as the cosecant of the angle of cut. cosecant 30 degrees is 2, and cosecant 90 degrees is 1.

questions.stem: Three bearings give a cocked hat about 0.3 nm across. A dangerous rock lies 0.4 nm from one corner on the seaward side. Which position should be used for safety?
options: The centre of the triangle
The corner farthest from the rock
The DR position
The corner nearest the rock
questions.explanation: When a danger is near, assume the worst. The ship could be at the corner closest to it, so plan as if she is there.

questions.stem: What does a large cocked hat tell you?
options: That the compass error is exactly zero
That the fix is exact at the centre
Some bearing, ID, conversion or plot is wrong
That the objects used are floating buoys
questions.explanation: A small hat is normal; a large one is a warning. Check identification, the compass error, arithmetic and plotting, and retake the bearings.

questions.stem: Why does a bearing of a floating buoy give only an estimated position?
options: Buoys have no charted position at all
It swings on its mooring, may be off station
Bearings of buoys are always reciprocal
Buoys are not visible at night
questions.explanation: A buoy moves on its watch circle. Use fixed objects for the fix and buoys only as a confirmation.

questions.stem: Why should the bearings be taken quickly and the time of each noted?
options: Because compass error changes with time of day
Because a bearing lasts only 10 minutes
She is moving, so delay shifts the lines
Because the objects move on the chart
questions.explanation: The lines are meant to cross at one place at one time. The longer the interval, the further the ship has moved.

questions.stem: A hand-bearing compass, held clear of iron, reads 080 degrees on a beacon. Variation is 16 degrees E. What true bearing is plotted?
options: 064 degrees
096 degrees
080 degrees
100 degrees
questions.explanation: A hand compass held clear of iron has no deviation. Add the easterly variation: 080 + 16 = 096. Subtracting (064) is true to magnetic.

questions.stem: Which set of objects would you choose for a three-bearing fix?
options: Three good marks about 120 degrees apart
Three objects within 20 degrees of each other
Two objects ahead and one buoy astern on the same line
Three objects all on one side, within 10 degrees
questions.explanation: With three lines, about 60 degrees between neighbouring lines (roughly 120 degrees between the outer two) gives the best fix and a hat that reveals error. Clustered objects give poor crossings.
